name: jigdo
desc: Tool to distribute very large files over the internet
why: Jigdo's template-based distribution of huge files from many mirrors is a clever, forgotten transfer scheme worth understanding.

brief.what_it_is: Jigdo (Jigsaw Download) is a command-line toolkit for distributing very large files, such as CD or DVD images, over the internet. The publisher runs jigdo-file on the image and on a set of source files. It produces a small human-readable .jigdo description file and a binary .template file. A user gives the .jigdo file to a download client, which fetches the pieces of the image from one or more mirrors and reassembles the exact image. The homepage says the goal is downloading images as easy as clicking a direct download link in a browser. The three executables named in the brew metadata are jigdo-file, jigdo-lite and jigdo-mirror. The homepage describes the tool family in general and does not document these three executables individually.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it exists to make downloading very large images as easy for users as a direct browser download link, while avoiding the hosting problems server administrators have with such large files. The man page adds that it was made primarily for ISO9660 and UDF images but could also serve large audio, video or software packages.
brief.how_it_works: jigdo-file scans the image with a rolling checksum inspired by rsync and finds the regions that match known input files. Matched data is left out of the template and replaced with a checksum reference, while unmatched data such as directory information is compressed into the template. The .jigdo file is an INI-style text file that maps each part's checksum to one or more labelled server locations, so mirrors can be added by editing it. Format v1 uses MD5 checksums. Format v2, added in 0.8.0, uses SHA256 and is not readable by pre-0.8.0 tools.

commands_seen.context: Man page text on the make-image command: it reads a .template and the available files and builds the image, which can be done in several passes, with the result written to imagename.tmp until complete.
Synopsis line from the jigdo-file(1) man page. Common commands are make-template, make-image and verify. make-template is the main command that creates the .jigdo and .template files.
Example from the man page for --match-exec. It runs a shell command for each matched file, here to create hard-link backups of matched files in a directory tree.

brief.install_notes: The homepage says most Linux users should install from their distribution, since Debian, Ubuntu and others package jigdo. Source tarballs, zip files and Windows binaries are on the download area, and all are PGP-signed with .sig files. Development code is at git.einval.com, on the 'upstream' branch. The homepage says building from source should be easy, and the author offers help with building or finding binaries for other platforms. The brew metadata gives no notes beyond the executable names.
brief.standout: The parts of an image can be any size and content, as long as each is one contiguous region of the image, and they can be stored on different mirrors. The user's client fetches a CD-sized ISO from an FTP tree of individual files and reassembles it byte-for-byte during the download. The mirror layout is a plain text file that can be edited without rebuilding the image.
brief.status: Maintained but slow-moving. The homepage was last updated January 2025. Its most recent news items are the 0.8.2 release on 3 August 2023 and Debian trixie switching to v2 files on 7 October 2023. The homepage links to a git repository for development, but I did not open it, so I cannot confirm recent commits.
brief.caveats: The man page says the jigdo download tool is 'NOT IMPLEMENTED YET', which conflicts with the homepage's description of Jigdo as the initial implementation; the man page text may be stale, so check the installed version. The default checksum is MD5, which the author calls no longer secure; SHA256 (v2) requires newer tools on the receiving end. The author says genisoimage support is deprecated and that he will not add v2 support there. The v2 xorriso support was described as 'coming very soon' with no date given. The homepage has no licence information. This brief covers only the homepage and one man page, not the source repository.
quotes: Jigsaw Download (for short "jigdo"), is a tool designed to ease the distribution of very large files over the internet, for example CD or DVD images.
His description of how jigdo works might be interesting - it's a very clever design!
Older versions of the tools will recognise a newer version of the format and fail gracefully, which is the best they can do.

judge.reason: Jigdo reconstructs huge images from matching files scattered across mirrors, a clever checksum-driven distribution scheme that opens a genuinely unusual door.

entry.title: jigdo
entry.tldr: Jigsaw Download rebuilds a huge CD or DVD image byte for byte from small pieces scattered across mirrors, using a text file you can edit.
entry.deeper_look:
Jigdo, short for Jigsaw Download, is a toolkit for distributing very large files, mainly ISO9660 and UDF disc images. The publisher runs `jigdo-file` over the image and the set of files it was built from. That produces two things: a small, human-readable `.jigdo` file and a binary `.template` file. A user hands the `.jigdo` file to a download client, which fetches the pieces from one or more mirrors and reassembles the exact image.

The trick is in the template. `jigdo-file` scans the image with a rolling checksum inspired by rsync and finds regions that match known input files. Matched data is left out and replaced with a checksum reference. Unmatched data, such as directory structures, is compressed into the template. The `.jigdo` file is INI-style text mapping each part's checksum to labelled server locations, so adding a mirror means editing a text file, not rebuilding the image.

The homepage says it exists to make downloading very large images as easy as clicking a direct link in a browser, without the hosting problems such files cause server administrators. A CD-sized ISO can be assembled from an ordinary FTP tree of individual files. The pieces can be any size, as long as each is one contiguous region of the image.

The idea underneath is content-addressed transfer: name data by its checksum, and it no longer matters where it comes from. That is a door into rsync, package mirrors and reproducible images.
entry.install:
brew install jigdo
# The homepage says most Linux users should install from their distribution instead; Debian and Ubuntu package it.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the commands: make-template builds the .jigdo and .template files, make-image rebuilds an image, verify checks one.
Reads a .template plus the files you have and builds the image, in several passes if needed, writing to imagename.tmp until complete.
Shows the options of the download front end that takes a .jigdo file and fetches the pieces.

entry.whats_unique: The mirror layout is a plain text file you can edit without touching the image, and the image is rebuilt byte for byte from ordinary files on ordinary servers.
entry.caveats: Slow-moving: the latest release noted is 0.8.2 from August 2023; the default MD5 checksums are called no longer secure by the author, and the SHA256 v2 format needs 0.8.0 or newer tools.
